### Invariant forms are cocycles, so the Killing 3-form gives nonzero H³

**Remember:** Invariant forms are closed and never exact on reductive Lie algebras.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Koszul wrote the differential on the Chevalley–Eilenberg algebra Λ𝔤\* as d = ½ Σ eⁱ ∧ θ(eᵢ). Here θ is the coadjoint action and (eᵢ), (eⁱ) are dual bases. So d is zero on 𝔤-invariant forms.

**Problem.** For a finite-dimensional reductive Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field of characteristic zero, H\*(𝔤;k) is isomorphic to the algebra of 𝔤-invariant forms in Λ𝔤\*. In particular, for semisimple 𝔤 the form ⟨x,\[y,z\]⟩ gives a nonzero class in H³(𝔤;k), so the vanishing of H¹ and H² stops at degree 3.

**How the definition helps.** Written in Koszul's form, the differential is visibly zero on invariant forms, so every invariant form is a cocycle at once. The work went into showing that invariant forms meet every class exactly once. This uses that 𝔤 acts trivially on cohomology and that Λ𝔤\* is completely reducible, so the noninvariant part is acyclic.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “For instance for 𝔤 a semisimple Lie algebra, there is the Killing form ⟨−,−⟩. The corresponding 3-cocycle is μ := ⟨−,\[−,−\]⟩ ∈ CE(𝔤)”

**Sources:**

- [J.-L. Koszul, Homologie et cohomologie des algèbres de Lie, Bull. Soc. Math. France 78 (1950) 65–127](https://doi.org/10.24033/bsmf.1410)

### Invariants in two stages give the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence

**Remember:** Take 𝔥-invariants, then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants, and derive the composite.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G40. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is the n-th right derived functor of the invariants functor that sends M to its 𝔤-invariants. For an ideal 𝔥 of 𝔤, taking 𝔤-invariants is the same as taking 𝔥-invariants and then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants.

**Problem.** For an ideal 𝔥 of a Lie algebra 𝔤 and a 𝔤-module M, there is a spectral sequence from H\*(𝔤/𝔥; H\*(𝔥;M)) to H\*(𝔤;M). Its low-degree terms give the five-term inflation-restriction exact sequence.

**How the definition helps.** With cohomology defined as a derived functor, the spectral sequence is Grothendieck's spectral sequence for a composite of two functors. The check is that 𝔥-invariants send injective 𝔤-modules to injective 𝔤/𝔥-modules, being right adjoint to the exact inflation functor. Restriction to 𝔥 also keeps injective modules, because U(𝔤) is free over U(𝔥) (our own). Hochschild and Serre instead built the sequence by filtering the cochain complex.

**nLab:** [Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hochschild-Serre+spectral+sequence). It says: “The invariants can be computed in two stages, hence as the composite of two functors”

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “the inflation-restriction sequence (namely, the 5-term sequence induced by the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence) associated with the exact sequence of ℕ-graded 𝔽-Lie algebras 0→I→ℱ→ℒ→0”

**Sources:**

- [G. Hochschild and J.-P. Serre, Cohomology of Lie algebras, Ann. of Math. 57 (1953) 591–603](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969740)

### Left-invariant forms make Lie algebra cohomology the cohomology of compact groups

**Remember:** Average forms over a compact group, and only Lie algebra data remain.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T10. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of a real Lie algebra 𝔤 is the exterior algebra Λ𝔤\* of alternating forms, with differential dω(x₀,…,xₙ) = Σ ± ω(\[xᵢ,xⱼ\], …). For a Lie group G it is exactly the complex of left-invariant differential forms on G with the de Rham differential.

**Problem.** For a compact connected Lie group G, the de Rham cohomology of G is isomorphic to the Lie algebra cohomology H\*(𝔤;ℝ). This fails without compactness: the group ℝ is contractible, but H¹ of its Lie algebra is ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** Because the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex is the complex of left-invariant forms, the theorem only says that invariant forms compute de Rham cohomology. The work went into the averaging argument. Integrating over G with Haar measure projects onto invariant forms. Translations act trivially on cohomology because G is connected.

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Using an averaging process, this complex can be replaced by the complex of left-invariant differential forms.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Relative cochains are invariant forms, so relative cohomology computes compact homogeneous spaces

**Remember:** Invariant forms on G/K are exactly the relative cochains.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T15. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 with subalgebra 𝔨, the relative cochains are the 𝔨-invariant elements of Λ(𝔤/𝔨)\*, with the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. Their cohomology is the relative Lie algebra cohomology H\*(𝔤,𝔨).

**Problem.** Let G be a compact connected Lie group and K a closed connected subgroup. Then the de Rham cohomology of G/K is isomorphic to H\*(𝔤,𝔨;ℝ).

**How the definition helps.** With this definition, a relative cochain is the value at the base point of a G-invariant form on G/K. So the relative complex is the complex of G-invariant forms. The work went into the averaging argument over the compact group G, as for G itself (our own summary).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “consisting of the 𝔥-invariant elements in the tensor product of V with the exterior algebra of the coset 𝔤/𝔥.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### The Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution makes cohomology vanish above the dimension

**Remember:** No alternating forms above dim 𝔤, so no cohomology there.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B35. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution of the trivial module k is the complex U(𝔤) ⊗ Λⁿ𝔤 of free U(𝔤)-modules, with a Koszul-type differential. Its Hom into M is the complex of alternating forms on 𝔤 with values in M.

**Problem.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 of finite dimension d over a field, Hⁿ(𝔤,M) = 0 for every module M and every n &gt; d. Hence Ext over U(𝔤) between any two modules vanishes above degree d, so U(𝔤) has global dimension at most d.

**How the definition helps.** With the Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution, the cochains in degree n are alternating n-forms, and there are none above degree d. The bound for all modules follows because Ext from N to M equals Lie algebra cohomology with coefficients in Hom(N,M) (our own). The work went into proving the resolution exact, which reduces by the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt filtration to the exactness of the Koszul complex of a polynomial ring.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “Lie algebra cohomology and homology were defined by Chevalley-Eilenberg with a help of concrete Koszul-type resolution”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### The Ext definition gives free Lie algebras cohomological dimension one

**Remember:** Tensor algebras have a two-term resolution, so free Lie algebras stop at H¹.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B01. arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is Extⁿ over the universal enveloping algebra U(𝔤) from the trivial module to M. For the free Lie algebra on a vector space V, the enveloping algebra is the tensor algebra T(V).

**Problem.** If 𝔣 is a free Lie algebra, then Hⁿ(𝔣,M) = 0 for every module M and every n ≥ 2. Conversely, an ℕ-graded Lie algebra L generated by its degree-one part with H²(L,𝔽) = 0 is free.

**How the definition helps.** With the Ext definition, one short projective resolution of the trivial module bounds all cohomology. Over T(V) the augmentation ideal is the free module T(V) ⊗ V, which gives the two-term resolution in the quote. The work went into the fact that U of a free Lie algebra is the tensor algebra, which follows from the two universal properties. The converse uses the inflation-restriction sequence for the kernel of the map from the free Lie algebra.

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “If ℒ is free, then H²(ℒ,𝔽)=0, since 0→𝒰(ℒ)⊗ℒ₁→𝒰(ℒ)→𝔽→0 is a projective resolution of the trivial 𝒰(ℒ)-module 𝔽.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras, arXiv:2201.03034](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034)

### The symmetric-space involution kills the differential on invariant forms

**Remember:** The involution has sign (−1)ᵏ, so d must be zero.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 53C35, 57T15. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A compact symmetric space is G/K with an involution σ of G whose fixed points contain K as an open subgroup. Then 𝔤 = 𝔨 ⊕ 𝔭, where σ is +1 on 𝔨 and −1 on 𝔭. The relative cochains are the K-invariant elements of Λ𝔭\*.

**Problem.** Let G/K be a compact symmetric space with G compact and connected. Then every G-invariant differential form on G/K is closed, so the de Rham cohomology of G/K is (Λ𝔭\*)ᴷ, the K-invariant forms on 𝔭 (Cartan).

**How the definition helps.** The involution acts on invariant k-forms by (−1)ᵏ, and it commutes with d. So for an invariant k-form ω, the form dω is multiplied both by (−1)ᵏ and by (−1)ᵏ⁺¹, so dω = 0 (our own). The work went into the theorem that G-invariant forms compute the cohomology of G/K, which needs averaging over the compact group G.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “consisting of the 𝔥-invariant elements in the tensor product of V with the exterior algebra of the coset 𝔤/𝔥.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Universal central extensions exist exactly for perfect Lie algebras, with kernel H₂

**Remember:** Only perfect algebras have a universal cover, and its kernel is H₂.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B55. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A central extension of a Lie algebra 𝔤 is a surjection 𝔢 → 𝔤 whose kernel lies in the center of 𝔢. A universal central extension is an initial object among central extensions of 𝔤. A Lie algebra is perfect when \[𝔤,𝔤\] = 𝔤.

**Problem.** A Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field has a universal central extension if and only if 𝔤 is perfect. Then the extension is unique up to unique isomorphism, and its kernel is the homology H₂(𝔤).

**How the definition helps.** Defining the universal extension as an initial object gives uniqueness up to unique isomorphism at once. Perfectness removes the abelian counterexample k: maps between split extensions k ⊕ V change by any linear map k → V, so none is initial (our own). For perfect 𝔤, the extension is Λ²𝔤 divided by the boundary image of Λ³𝔤, mapped to 𝔤 by x∧y ↦ \[x,y\]. Its kernel is H₂(𝔤) by the Chevalley–Eilenberg chain complex (our own summary).

**nLab:** [universal central extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+central+extension). It says: “the universal central extension is, if it exists, the initial object in the category of central extensions of that object.”

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_extension). It says: “By universality, it is easy to conclude that such universal central extensions are unique up to isomorphism.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Witt brackets inherit Jacobi

**Remember:** Use commutators of operators and Jacobi comes from composition.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B66 (Lie algebras of vector fields and related (super) algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A derivation is a linear operator D satisfying D(fg) = D(f)g + fD(g). The complex Witt algebra consists of derivations of complex Laurent polynomials, which allow negative integer powers of the variable. Its bracket is the operator commutator \[D,E\] = DE − ED. Another presentation gives a bracket table for a basis indexed by integers.

**Problem.** The bracket on the complex Witt algebra obeys the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** Operator composition is associative, so the Jacobi sum cancels in pairs before any basis calculation (our own). The work moves to showing that commutators preserve derivations and that the Laurent monomial derivations give the usual basis and bracket (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Witt algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_algebra). It says: “the Lie algebra of derivations of the ring C\[z,z⁻¹\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Realizations of singular Cartan matrices keep simple roots linearly independent

**Remember:** Enlarge the space 𝔥 until the simple roots stop colliding.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B67 (Kac-Moody (super)algebras; extended affine Lie algebras; toroidal Lie algebras), 17B22. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A generalized Cartan matrix C is an n × n integer matrix of rank r, with 2 on the diagonal and nonpositive entries elsewhere. Also cᵢⱼ = 0 exactly when cⱼᵢ = 0. A realization is a complex vector space 𝔥 of dimension 2n − r with independent vectors αᵢ∨, the simple coroots. It also has independent linear forms αᵢ on 𝔥, the simple roots, with αᵢ(αⱼ∨) = cⱼᵢ.

**Problem.** Every generalized Cartan matrix has a realization, unique up to isomorphism. The Kac–Moody algebra built from it by generators and relations splits into 𝔥 and root spaces, the common eigenspaces of 𝔥. Every root is a sum of simple roots with integer coefficients all of one sign.

**How the definition helps.** Choosing the dimension 2n − r leaves room for both the simple roots and the simple coroots to be independent, even when C is singular. Take the affine matrix with rows (2, −2) and (−2, 2), of rank 1 (our own). On a space of dimension 2, its two simple roots would satisfy α₁ = −α₂, so positive and negative roots could not be told apart (our own). The root space decomposition is still a real theorem, proved in Kac's book (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra). It says: “The vector space 𝔥 has dimension 2n − r … The sets {αᵢ} and {αᵢ∨} are linearly independent”

**Sources:**

- [Moody, R. V. (1967). Lie algebras associated with generalized Cartan matrices. Bulletin of the AMS 73, 217–222.](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1967-11688-4)
- [Kac, V. G. (1968). Simple irreducible graded Lie algebras of finite growth. Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 2.](https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1968v002n06ABEH000729)

### Locality and translation give skew symmetry

**Remember:** Commute on the vacuum, then translate and cancel the common power.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In the locality presentation of a vertex algebra, a state u has an operator series Y(u,z), called its field. For each pair of states, some nonnegative power of z − w kills the commutator of their fields. The translation operator T differentiates fields by commutator and kills the vacuum. Applying a field to the vacuum gives a power series whose constant term is its state.

**Problem.** For all states u and v, skew symmetry gives Y(u,z)v = exp(zT)Y(v,−z)u.

**How the definition helps.** Locality lets us exchange the two fields on the vacuum after clearing their poles. Our own calculation uses translation to write the field of v on the vacuum as exp(wT)v. Moving translations past fields changes their arguments by the corresponding shifts. After clearing poles we can set w to zero and cancel the common power of z. The formal Jacobi identity gives another presentation, whose equivalence requires a separate proof.

**Wikipedia:** [Vertex operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_operator_algebra). It says: “(skew-symmetry) Y(u,z)v=eᶻᵀY(v,−z)u”

**Sources:**

- [Frenkel and Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)

### One character forces modular invariance

**Remember:** One character and trivial translation force trivial modular action.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a vertex operator algebra holomorphic when it is simple, rational, self-dual, C₂-cofinite and of CFT type, and its vacuum module is its only simple module. Its character is the sum over n of dim(Vₙ) times q to the power n − c/24, with q = exp(2πiτ) and c the central charge.

**Problem.** If a holomorphic vertex operator algebra has central charge divisible by 24, its character is invariant under the modular group.

**How the definition helps.** Divisibility by 24 removes the scalar acquired under the translation T taking τ to τ + 1. Zhu's theorem and the single simple module make the character span a one-dimensional representation. Since T acts trivially, the relation S² = (ST)³ forces the inversion S to act trivially. Our own counterexample is the holomorphic vertex algebra of the E₈ lattice, with central charge eight, where T acts by exp(−2πi/3).

**Paper or page:** [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3), [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3). It says: “Then 𝔠𝔥\[V\] is a right Γ-submodule of 𝔉.”

**Sources:**

- [Cameron Franc, Geoffrey Mason, Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3)
- [Yongchang Zhu, Modular invariance of characters of vertex operator algebras](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0894-0347-96-00182-8)
- [Chongying Dong, Vertex Algebras Associated with Even Lattices](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1993.1217)

### Truncation excludes evaluation modules

**Remember:** Without truncation, a current series need not act as a field.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures). arXiv math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Start with the centrally extended loop algebra of a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with a fixed invariant form. The level is the scalar by which the central element acts. A module is restricted if, for each current and each vector, all sufficiently high modes of that current kill the vector.

**Problem.** At level k, restriction to current modes identifies modules of the universal affine vertex algebra with restricted level-k modules of the centrally extended loop algebra.

**How the definition helps.** Restrictedness is exactly the requirement that each current field have only finitely many pole terms on each vector. Our own counterexample evaluates loops at 1 on a nontrivial representation and gives the central element action zero. Every mode of a given current then acts by the same operator, violating truncation. The affine reconstruction theorem extends restricted current actions uniquely to fields for all states. Take the identity twist and ε = 0 in the cited proposition.

**Paper or page:** [A unified construction of vertex algebras from infinite-dimensional Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16744v1). It says: “Γσ-equivariant φε-coordinated quasi Vℒ̂(𝔟)-modules are exactly restricted ℒ̂(𝔟,σ)-modules.”

**Sources:**

- [Fulin Chen, Xiaoling Liao, Shaobin Tan, Qing Wang, A unified construction of vertex algebras from infinite-dimensional Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16744v1)
- [Edward Frenkel and David Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)

### Unimodularity removes extra modules

**Remember:** Only the vacuum coset survives when the lattice equals its dual.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a positive definite even lattice L to build its lattice vertex operator algebra. Require L to be unimodular, so the lattice equals the dual lattice of vectors pairing integrally with L. Evenness by itself only requires that squared lengths are even integers.

**Problem.** An even positive definite lattice gives a holomorphic vertex operator algebra exactly when it is unimodular. Here holomorphic means that the vacuum module is the only simple module with finite-dimensional weight spaces and weights bounded below.

**How the definition helps.** Unimodularity leaves just one label in the classification of simple modules. Dong’s theorem labels them by cosets of L in its dual, with the zero coset giving the vacuum. Our own example takes a lattice generated by a vector of squared length two. Half that vector generates the dual, giving a second coset and a second simple module.

**Wikipedia:** [Vertex operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_operator_algebra). It says: “Lattice vertex algebras are canonically attached to double covers of even integral lattices”

**Sources:**

- [Frenkel and Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)
- [Chongying Dong, Vertex Algebras Associated with Even Lattices](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1993.1217)

### Parity signs give the supercommutator its Jacobi identity

**Remember:** Two odd inputs change subtraction to addition.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B70 (Graded Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Split an associative algebra into even and odd subspaces, with multiplication adding degrees modulo two. For inputs of definite parity, the supercommutator is xy − yx unless both inputs are odd. For two odd inputs it is xy + yx. Extend by bilinearity.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic zero, the supercommutator defines a Lie superalgebra on any associative algebra graded by parity.

**How the definition helps.** The parity sign cancels the terms in the signed Jacobi identity after associativity removes parentheses (our own). In two-by-two matrices, take diagonal matrices as even and off-diagonal matrices as odd (our own). The ordinary commutator of the two off-diagonal matrix units is nonzero and changes sign when they exchange places (our own). A Lie superalgebra requires symmetry on two odd inputs (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Superalgebras with Homogeneous structures of Lie type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00618). It says: “Any Super-associative superalgebra is a Super-Lie admissible superalgebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Jacobi sum kills cubes

**Remember:** Put the same element into all three slots of the Jacobi sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C05 (Identities and free Jordan structures). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Jacobi–Jordan algebra has a commutative bilinear product satisfying (xy)z + (yz)x + (zx)y = 0. Among commutative algebras over fields of characteristic other than two or three, the equivalent cube law is (xx)x = 0.

**Problem.** For a commutative algebra over a field of characteristic other than two or three, the Jacobi identity holds exactly when all cubes vanish.

**How the definition helps.** The cube definition makes vanishing immediate, while the three-input definition makes the Jacobi identity immediate. Our own check puts x in all three slots of that identity and divides by three. Conversely, expand the cube of x + y + z. Subtract the three pairwise sum cubes and add back the individual cubes. What remains is twice the Jacobi sum, which therefore vanishes when all cubes vanish and two is invertible. Our own example in characteristic three is the field with three elements. Its Jacobi sum vanishes, yet the cube of 1 is 1.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology and deformations of Jacobi-Jordan algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12364v1). It says: “such that x³ = 0, ∀ x ∈ J.”

**Sources:**

- [Amir Baklouti, Said Benayadi, Abdenacer Makhlouf, Sabeur Mansour. Cohomology and deformations of Jacobi-Jordan algebras, Proposition 2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12364v1)
- [Dietrich Burde and Alice Fialowski. Jacobi–Jordan algebras (2014).](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.laa.2014.07.034)

### Quadratic operators produce inner ideals

**Remember:** One sandwich operator produces a subspace closed under more sandwiches.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C10 (Structure theory for Jordan algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a quadratic Jordan algebra, Q(a)b is quadratic in a and linear in b. For matrices, Q(a)b = aba. One defining identity is Q(Q(a)b) = Q(a)Q(b)Q(a), where adjacent operators compose. A subspace B is an inner ideal if Q(b)c belongs to B whenever b belongs to B and c is arbitrary.

**Problem.** For every a in a quadratic Jordan algebra, the image of Q(a) is an inner ideal.

**How the definition helps.** The defining identity puts Q(a) last in the order of application, so Q(Q(a)b)c lies in its image (our own). Starting with a binary Jordan product instead requires proving this identity for the associated operators (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Jordan_algebra). It says: “For given b, the image of Q(b) is an inner ideal”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating associators force flexibility

**Remember:** An alternating associator vanishes whenever an input repeats.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The associator measures the difference (xy)z − x(yz). The usual alternative laws say that it vanishes when the first two inputs agree or the last two agree. Equivalently, it is alternating, meaning it vanishes whenever any two inputs agree.

**Problem.** Every alternative algebra satisfies (xy)x = x(yx), even in characteristic two.

**How the definition helps.** The first and third inputs agree, so the alternating associator is zero. The work is to derive full alternation from the two original identities by expanding sums of inputs. Our own counterexample uses three basis elements e, f, g over the two-element field. Set ee = f and fe = g, with all other basis products zero. Its only nonzero basis associator is at (e,e,e), so it is unchanged by swaps. In characteristic two this satisfies the sign rule, but flexibility fails.

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “By definition, a multilinear map is alternating if it vanishes whenever two of its arguments are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Artin’s theorem reverses unit products

**Remember:** Put two units in one associative algebra, then reverse their order.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebra is alternative when x(xy) = (xx)y and (yx)x = y(xx). Artin’s theorem gives an equivalent definition. Any two elements generate an associative subalgebra. A unit is an element with a two-sided multiplicative inverse.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional unital alternative algebra over a field, a product of two units is a unit. Its inverse is the product of their inverses in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** Once both inverses lie in the associative subalgebra generated by the two units and 1, ordinary multiplication verifies the inverse formula (our own). For either unit x, consider the finite-dimensional subalgebra generated by x and 1 (our own). The inverse law x⁻¹(xv) = v makes multiplication by x injective there, hence surjective (our own). A preimage of 1 equals x⁻¹ by the same law (our own). Artin’s theorem and the inverse law supply the steps beyond associative multiplication (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “If x and y are invertible then xy is also invertible with inverse (xy)⁻¹ = y⁻¹x⁻¹.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Commutative alternative algebras associate without three-torsion

**Remember:** Three times the associator vanishes, so rule out three-torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The associator measures the failure of associativity by A(x,y,z) = (xy)z − x(yz). An algebra is alternative when its associator vanishes whenever two inputs agree. Its additive group has no three-torsion when 3a = 0 forces a = 0.

**Problem.** A commutative alternative algebra without additive three-torsion is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Commutativity cancels the cyclic sum of associators, and alternation makes all three terms equal (our own). Thus 3A(x,y,z) = 0. Over the field with three elements, take a commutative algebra with basis x,y,z,u,v,w,t (our own). Set xy=u, yz=v, zx=w, uz=t and wy=−t, with other unordered basis products zero (our own). Only permutations of x,y,z have nonzero associator (our own). Cyclic orders give t and reversed orders give −t, so the associator alternates without vanishing identically (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426). It says: “For each a,b,c ∈ K, we have 3((ab)c − a(bc)) = 0. Hence, K is associative if K has no 3-torsion.”

**Sources:**

- [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426)

### Pre-Lie left multiplication preserves brackets

**Remember:** Left multiplication takes each bracket to the bracket of operators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D25 (Lie-admissible algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write L(x) for multiplication on the left by x. Define a left pre-Lie algebra by requiring L(x)L(y) − L(y)L(x) = L(xy − yx). The usual definition instead requires (xy)z − x(yz) to be symmetric in x and y.

**Problem.** In a left pre-Lie algebra, the bracket \[x,y\] = xy − yx makes the algebra a Lie algebra. Left multiplication represents it by linear operators whose commutator equals L(\[x,y\]).

**How the definition helps.** The defining operator equation says exactly that left multiplication preserves brackets. Our own check recovers the usual symmetry by applying both sides to z and rearranging. To prove the Lie bracket identity, expand \[x,\[y,z\]\] + \[y,\[z,x\]\] + \[z,\[x,y\]\]. The terms cancel in pairs of equal associators, the differences between the two ways to group three factors.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5). It says: “Furthermore, the map adᴸ: L → gl(L) with x ↦ Lₓ gives a representation of the Lie algebra (L,\[·,·\]).”

**Sources:**

- [A. Ben Hassine, T. Chtioui, M. Elhamdadi, S. Mabrouk. Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras, Lemma 2.2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5)

### Dendriform sums are associative

**Remember:** Add the three split laws to recover the associative law.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A30 (Nonassociative algebras satisfying other identities). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dendriform dialgebra has bilinear operations ≺ and ≻ with sum ∗. The first law is (x ≺ y) ≺ z = x ≺ (y ∗ z). The second is (x ≻ y) ≺ z = x ≻ (y ≺ z). The third is (x ∗ y) ≻ z = x ≻ (y ≻ z).

**Problem.** The sum of the two dendriform operations is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Adding the three defining laws gives the associative law for ∗. Our own comparison starts from the usual test, expanding (x ∗ y) ∗ z and x ∗ (y ∗ z). The three laws already match all terms in these expansions. The work lies in finding operations that satisfy each law separately.

**nLab:** [dendriform algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dendriform+algebra). It says: “The sum of the two binary operations is an associative operation.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Louis Loday. Dialgebras (2001).](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-45328-8_2)

### Zinbiel symmetrization is associative

**Remember:** Rewrite a left pair as the sum of both right orders.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A30 (Nonassociative algebras satisfying other identities). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Zinbiel algebra has a bilinear product written by juxtaposition, with (xy)z = x(yz + zy). Use the symmetrized product x\*y = xy + yx instead of the original product.

**Problem.** The symmetrized product of a Zinbiel algebra is commutative and associative.

**How the definition helps.** Symmetrizing supplies both orders needed by the Zinbiel rule, so both groupings give x(yz+zy) + y(zx+xz) + z(xy+yx) (our own). For an example over the rationals, take basis a,b,c and products aa=b, ab=c, ba=2c, with all other basis products zero (our own). Only the triple a,a,a gives a nonzero side of the Zinbiel rule, and both sides equal 2c (our own). Yet (aa)a = 2c and a(aa) = c (our own).

**nLab:** [Zinbiel algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Zinbiel+algebra). It says: “A Zinbiel algebra or dual Leibniz algebra (in Vec) is a nonassociative algebra with a product satisfying (xy)z = x(zy + yz),”

**Paper or page:** [On Ternary F-manifold Algebras and their Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13600). It says: “Then (A,·) is a commutative associative algebra, where x·y = x⋄y + y⋄x.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Leibniz deformation maps give complements

**Remember:** A complement is a graph, and the bracket must stay on it.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A32 (Leibniz algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A left Leibniz algebra has a bilinear bracket for which each map y ↦ \[x,y\] obeys the product rule. Split its vector space as G ⊕ H. The graph of a linear map r from H to G consists of the pairs (r(u),u). Call r a deformation map if each bracket of graph elements has G component equal to r applied to its H component.

**Problem.** The deformation maps correspond to the subalgebras complementary to G as vector spaces.

**How the definition helps.** The component equation says precisely that the graph contains every bracket of two graph elements. Our own comparison starts with a complementary subspace and tests closure there. Projection onto H identifies that subspace with H and gives a unique graph. Computing the two components of the bracket supplies the equation for its map.

**Paper or page:** [Deformation maps in proto-twilled Leibniz algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18599v2). It says: “A linear map r : h → g is a deformation map if and only if the graph Gr(r) = {(r(u), u) \| u ∈ h} is a subalgebra of the Leibniz algebra (G, \[ , \]).”

**Sources:**

- [Apurba Das, Suman Majhi, Ramkrishna Mandal. Deformation maps in proto-twilled Leibniz algebras, Proposition 4.1.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18599v2)

### Nijenhuis operators preserve deformed products

**Remember:** The Nijenhuis equation says which product the operator preserves.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A36 (Automorphisms, derivations, other operators (nonassociative rings and algebras)). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a linear operator N on an algebra, set x ∗ y = N(x)y + xN(y) − N(xy). Call N a Nijenhuis operator when N(x ∗ y) = N(x)N(y). The usual form expands the left side as N(N(x)y + xN(y)) − N²(xy). In a left pre-Jacobi–Jordan algebra, the sum (xy)z + x(yz) changes sign when x and y are swapped.

**Problem.** Let N be a Nijenhuis operator on a left pre-Jacobi–Jordan algebra. Then x ∗ y is again a left pre-Jacobi–Jordan product, and N is a morphism from the new algebra to the original one.

**How the definition helps.** The defining equation for N says directly that it preserves the new product. Our own comparison uses the expanded operator equation, which hides the product that N preserves. Proposition 5.3 also proves that the new product satisfies the defining algebra identity. When N has a nonzero kernel, preservation of multiplication alone cannot prove this.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomologies and linear deformations of pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03076v1). It says: “is left pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebra and N is a morphism”

**Sources:**

- [Sylvain Attan, Nabil Oro Djibril. Cohomologies and linear deformations of pre-Jacobi-Jordan algebras, Proposition 5.3.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03076v1)

### Faithful even brackets enable reconstruction

**Remember:** Keep only the even operators that come from odd brackets.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17A40 (Ternary compositions). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Grade an ordinary Lie algebra into even and odd subspaces, with brackets adding degrees modulo two. Its odd part has a ternary operation T(x,y,z) = \[\[x,y\],z\], called its Lie triple product. Reconstruct the even part as the span of the operators z ↦ T(x,y,z).

**Problem.** This construction recovers the original graded Lie algebra if brackets of odd elements span the even part and its action on odd elements is faithful. Faithful means only zero acts by the zero operator.

**How the definition helps.** The spanning condition gives every even action as a sum of triple operators, and faithfulness identifies the even part with their span (our own). Operator commutators recover even brackets by Jacobi, and T(x,y,−) represents the bracket of two odd elements (our own). An abelian graded Lie algebra with a nonzero even part loses that part under reconstruction.

**nLab:** [Lie triple system](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+triple+system). It says: “any abelian ℤ/2-graded Lie algebra (hence with vanishing Lie bracket) converted into a Lie triple system and back into a ℤ/2-graded Lie algebra has a zero-dimensional space of even elements.”

**Sources:**

- [Oleg Smirnov, Imbedding of Lie triple systems into Lie algebras (2011)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jalgebra.2011.06.011)

### Octonions are associative inside a suitably twisted graded category

**Remember:** The octonions are associative once the surrounding category has the right associator.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17A75 (Composition algebras), 18M05, 18A50. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The octonions are the real group algebra of ℤ₂³ with its multiplication twisted by a function ω on pairs of group elements. Here ω is not a 2-cocycle, so its coboundary φ = ∂ω is a 3-cocycle that is not identically 1. So φ defines a non-identity associator on the category of ℤ₂³-graded real vector spaces.

**Problem.** In the category of ℤ₂³-graded real vector spaces with associator φ, the octonions are an associative algebra (a monoid object).

**How the definition helps.** Change the associator of the surrounding category, and the octonions become associative there by construction. Albuquerque and Majid show that the quaternions come from a genuine 2-cocycle on ℤ₂², so they are associative in the usual sense. Our own note: φ is a coboundary, so it is trivial as a cohomology class, but as a function it is not identically 1, so the associator is not the identity. The nLab says that the similar pattern for the sedenions is not proven.

**nLab:** [Cayley-Dickson construction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cayley-Dickson+construction). It says: “In the case of the octonions, these are better regarded as associative up to a nontrivial cocycle.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Albuquerque, S. Majid, Quasialgebra structure of the octonions, J. Algebra 220 (1999) 188–224](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1998.7850)

### Ihara brackets inherit Jacobi

**Remember:** Take commutators of derivations together with their conjugating elements.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 11M32. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In the free Lie algebra on x and y, let D(a) be the derivation sending x to zero and y to \[y,a\]. A derivation obeys the product rule for brackets. Pair each a with D(a) in the Lie algebra combining elements with derivations acting on them.

**Problem.** The Ihara bracket {a,b} = \[a,b\] + D(a)b − D(b)a satisfies the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** Our own construction realizes the formula as a bracket of pairs, so it inherits Jacobi without expanding a triple bracket. Checking the two generators gives \[D(a),D(b)\] = D({a,b}). This identity proves that the pairs are closed under the bracket.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630). It says: “The pair (𝔣₂, {−,−}) is a Lie algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Annika Burmester, Niclas Confurius and Ulf Kühn, AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630)

### Paired derivations prove Ihara Jacobi

**Remember:** Pair each Lie element with the derivation it determines.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 11M32. arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let L be the free Lie algebra on x and y, generated using brackets subject only to the Lie identities. A derivation acts on a bracket by acting on each input in turn and adding. For f in L define dᶠ by dᶠ(x) = 0 and dᶠ(y) = \[y,f\]. Set {f,g} = \[f,g\] + dᶠ(g) − dᵍ(f), the Ihara bracket.

**Problem.** The Ihara bracket satisfies the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** The bracket is the first coordinate of the ordinary Lie bracket on pairs of Lie elements and derivations. In our own proof, the generator calculation gives \[dᶠ,dᵍ\] = d of the Ihara bracket. Thus the pairs (f,dᶠ) form a subalgebra of the semidirect product, which combines the Lie algebra with its derivations. The generator calculation carries the work that a direct Jacobi expansion would repeat.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “The pair (𝔣₂, {−,−}) is a Lie algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Category O keeps Verma modules while staying abelian and Noetherian

**Remember:** Big enough for Verma modules, small enough to be abelian.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)), 17B55. arXiv math.RT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let 𝔤 be a complex semisimple Lie algebra with a Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 and positive part 𝔫. Category O consists of the finitely generated 𝔤-modules that are direct sums of their 𝔥-weight spaces and in which each vector generates a finite-dimensional 𝔫-submodule.

**Problem.** Category O is an abelian category with enough projectives. Every object is Noetherian and has finite-dimensional weight spaces. It contains all Verma modules and all finite-dimensional modules.

**How the definition helps.** The three conditions are weak enough to admit the infinite-dimensional Verma modules but strong enough for finiteness properties. The category of all 𝔤-modules is too large to give these properties, and finite-dimensional modules alone leave out the Verma modules (our own). Inside category O, one can ask how often each irreducible module occurs in a Verma module (our own). BGG reciprocity and the Kazhdan–Lusztig conjectures, now theorems, answer this question, and their proofs use geometry of the flag variety (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Category O](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Category_O), [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module). It says: “Each module in category O has finite-dimensional weight spaces. … Each module in category O is a Noetherian module. … O is an abelian category.”

**Sources:**

- [Bernstein, I. N., Gelfand, I. M., Gelfand, S. I. (1976). Category of 𝔤-modules. Functional Analysis and Its Applications 10, 87–92.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01077933)

### Root groupoids give Lie superalgebras a Weyl group substitute with Coxeter relations

**Remember:** Let reflections move between root data, not only within one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B22 (Root systems), 17B67, 20F55. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A groupoid is a category in which every map is invertible. The root groupoid has root data as objects; a root datum records a choice of simple roots and their pairings. Its maps are generated by reflections and other moves, subject to relations. A reflection may change the root data, so it can be a map between two different objects.

**Problem.** The skeleton of each connected component of the root groupoid, a graph that generalizes the Cayley graph of the Weyl group, has the Coxeter property. For Kac–Moody Lie algebras this recovers the fact that the Weyl group is a Coxeter group.

**How the definition helps.** In a groupoid a reflection can start and end at different objects, so one graph can record the moves that change the root data. In our own explanation, odd reflections of Lie superalgebras change the root data. So a single group acting on one fixed root datum cannot record them. The groupoid makes the Coxeter statement possible to state. Proving the Coxeter property of the skeleton is still the paper's main work.

**Paper or page:** [Root groupoid and related Lie superalgebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06253v4). It says: “We establish the Coxeter property of the skeleton generalizing in this way the fact that the Weyl group of a Kac-Moody Lie algebra is Coxeter.”

**Sources:**

- [Maria Gorelik, Vladimir Hinich, Vera Serganova, Root groupoid and related Lie superalgebras, arXiv:2209.06253 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06253v4)

### The five-cycle gives associator reversal

**Remember:** Forgetting one vertex leaves only the two reversed factors.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B37 (Quantum groups (quantized enveloping algebras) and related deformations). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a field of characteristic zero, take a series Φ in two noncommuting letters whose value becomes one when the letters commute. Require Φ to be group-like, meaning its coproduct equals Φ ⊗ Φ when each letter splits as x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x. Use symmetric generators tᵢⱼ on distinct vertices with zero sum at each vertex and commuting generators on disjoint pairs. The five-cycle equation reads Φ(t₁₂,t₂₃)Φ(t₃₄,t₄₅)Φ(t₅₁,t₁₂)Φ(t₂₃,t₃₄)Φ(t₄₅,t₅₁) = 1.

**Problem.** Every such solution satisfies Φ(x,y)Φ(y,x) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** The five-cycle equation gives reversal by forgetting vertex five. In our own calculation, set its generators to zero and send t₁₂ and t₂₃ to x and y. The remaining vertex sums force t₃₄ to x. Each factor with a zero argument is one because a single letter commutes with itself. Only Φ(x,y) and Φ(y,x) survive. Furusho proves the equivalence with the original pentagon equation.

**nLab:** [Drinfeld associator](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld+associator). It says: “The pentagon equation”

**Sources:**

- [Hidekazu Furusho, Pentagon and hexagon equations, Annals of Mathematics 171 (2010), 545–556](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2010/171-1/p13)

### Torsors give rational associators

**Remember:** The torsor passes from a complex solution to a rational one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B37 (Quantum groups (quantized enveloping algebras) and related deformations). arXiv math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** An associator is a formal series in two noncommuting letters satisfying Drinfeld’s equations for consistent changes of parentheses and crossings. Fix a nonzero rational value μ for the crossing parameter. The solutions form a torsor, a space where exactly one group element carries any chosen point to any other. The acting group is built degree by degree from groups of upper triangular matrices with ones on the diagonal.

**Problem.** A Drinfeld associator over ℚ exists for each nonzero rational μ.

**How the definition helps.** The torsor description reduces rational existence to lifting points one degree at a time. Drinfeld constructs a complex solution by integration, and rescaling the letters gives the required parameter. His torsor theorem identifies the groups controlling successive lifts. In our own explanation, each lifting problem is a torsor under a rational vector group. Such a torsor has a rational point. Compatible lifts in all degrees give the rational series.

**nLab:** [Drinfeld associator](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Drinfeld+associator). It says: “An explicit associator over ℂ was constructed by Drinfeld from the monodromy of a universal version of the Knizhnik-Zamolodchikov equation.”

### Graphs differentiate Rota–Baxter operators

**Remember:** Differentiate the graph to get the graph of the derivative.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B38 (Yang-Baxter equations and Rota-Baxter operators). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let a Lie group G act smoothly by automorphisms on a Lie group H. Their semidirect product multiplies pairs using this action. A smooth map from H to G is a relative Rota–Baxter operator if its graph is a subgroup of that product. For Lie algebras, the corresponding graph must be a subalgebra of the semidirect product.

**Problem.** The derivative at the identity of a relative Rota–Baxter operator on Lie groups is a relative Rota–Baxter operator on their Lie algebras.

**How the definition helps.** Taking the tangent space at the identity turns the subgroup graph into the graph of the derivative. A Lie subgroup has a Lie subalgebra as its tangent space (our own). The work lies in proving both graph tests equivalent to the usual operator equations (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On the integration of relative Rota-Baxter Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23547). It says: “Then a smooth map ℬ: H → G is a relative Rota-Baxter operator if and only if the graph Gr(ℬ) = {(ℬ(h), h) \| h ∈ H} is a Lie subgroup”

**Sources:**

- [On the integration of relative Rota-Baxter Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.23547)

### Odd squares need another rule

**Remember:** In characteristic three, one odd triple must vanish on its own.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Lie superalgebra has even and odd subspaces, and brackets add degrees modulo two. Swapping bracket inputs changes the sign unless both are odd. Over a field of characteristic three, use the convention that also requires \[\[x,x\],x\] = 0 for odd x.

**Problem.** With this extra axiom, each odd x generates the subalgebra spanned by x and \[x,x\].

**How the definition helps.** The extra axiom kills the bracket between the two generators of the span (our own). The even element \[x,x\] brackets to zero with itself (our own). Without the axiom, take odd basis elements x,z and an even basis element y over the field with three elements (our own). Set \[x,x\]=y, \[y,x\]=z and \[x,y\]=−z, with every other basis bracket zero (our own). Only three copies of x can contribute to a Jacobi sum, and their three equal terms sum to zero (our own). Here x generates all three dimensions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie superalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_superalgebra). It says: “\[\[x,x\],x\] = 0 for \|x\| = 1 (if 3 is invertible this follows automatically).”

### Coalgebra conjugation preserves Koszul brackets

**Remember:** Conjugate the operator once to transport all its brackets.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 81T70. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let A be a graded commutative unital algebra over a characteristic-zero field. Extend a homogeneous operator D killing 1 to the symmetric coalgebra by applying D to each factor in turn with the graded signs. Let E be the coalgebra automorphism whose component from n factors to one multiplies those factors. Define the Koszul brackets as the one-output components of K(D) = E⁻¹ D̃ E, where D̃ denotes the extension.

**Problem.** For operators D and T killing 1, K(\[D,T\]) = \[K(D),K(T)\], where the bracket is the commutator with the graded sign.

**How the definition helps.** Conjugation preserves commutators, so the definition avoids expanding a separate signed product formula for every bracket (our own). The initial extension preserves commutators because terms acting on different factors cancel (our own). Identifying the resulting components with the usual Koszul brackets requires expanding the automorphism and its inverse (our own).

### Curvature detects obstructed lifts

**Remember:** Lift once, then test whether the curvature is a differential.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A differential graded Lie algebra has a bracket respecting degrees and a degree-raising differential d satisfying d² = 0 and the signed product rule. A degree-one element a has curvature da + \[a,a\]/2 and is a Maurer–Cartan element when this vanishes. A central extension is a surjective map of such algebras whose kernel brackets to zero with everything.

**Problem.** Let 𝔤̂ → 𝔤 be a central extension of nilpotent differential graded Lie algebras over a field of characteristic zero, with kernel K. Let â be any degree-one lift of a Maurer–Cartan element of 𝔤. Some lift has zero curvature exactly when the curvature of â equals db for some b in K.

**How the definition helps.** Adding a kernel element changes the curvature only by its differential, so subtracting b removes curvature db (our own). The curvature lies in the kernel because its image downstairs is zero (our own). The graded Jacobi identity shows that its differential vanishes (our own). Its class modulo differentials therefore measures the obstruction independently of the chosen lift.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Positive Energy Representations of Groups of Jets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10390). It says: “\[h\] ∈ H²(K) is independent of the lift”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Positive Energy Representations of Groups of Jets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10390)

### Lie n-algebras let higher cohomology classify extensions

**Remember:** H² gives Lie algebras, H³ gives Lie 2-algebras, and so on.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 17B56. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Lie n-algebra is an L∞-algebra concentrated in degrees 0 to n−1. An L∞-algebra is a graded space with brackets of every arity that satisfy higher Jacobi identities. The string Lie 2-algebra of a simple 𝔤 is the one built from the Killing 3-form.

**Problem.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 and a module M, Lie 2-algebras with 𝔤 in degree 0, M in degree 1, zero differential and the given action correspond, up to equivalence, to classes in H³(𝔤;M) (Baez–Crans). For simple 𝔤 the class of the Killing 3-form gives the string Lie 2-algebra.

**How the definition helps.** With the L∞ definition, such a Lie 2-algebra has one extra datum, a ternary bracket from Λ³𝔤 to M. The higher Jacobi identity for this bracket is exactly the 3-cocycle condition, which extends the classical fact that H² classifies abelian extensions (our own). The work went into showing that equivalences of Lie 2-algebras change the cocycle by a coboundary.

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “any element of the cohomology group Hⁿ⁺¹(𝔤; M) gives an equivalence class of ways to extend the Lie algebra 𝔤 to a "Lie n-algebra" with 𝔤 in grade zero and M in grade n−1.”
